The White-throated tyrannulet (Mecocerculus leucophrys) is a small-bodied insectivore inhabiting montane Andean forests, where it exhibits a life history finely tuned to cool, productive environments. Field measurements indicate that newly hatched chicks emerge with an initial wet body mass of 1.4 grams [Ww0 = 1.4 grams], a value consistent with the altricial developmental mode typical of tyrannid flycatchers. This modest starting mass, combined with the relatively brief nestling period, reflects the species' strategy of rapid post-hatching growth. This basal metabolic rate is comparatively high among related tyrannulet species of similar body mass, likely reflecting the energetic cost of maintaining homeothermy in a thermally challenging environment. Such a metabolic strategy is also evident in comparisons with other Andean tyrannids, where higher mass-specific oxygen consumption correlates with reduced body size and increased thermal conductance.

As the juvenile bird matures, physiological and morphological changes signal the approach of reproductive capability. Data collected from field studies indicate that the time since birth at puberty, representing the onset of gonadal maturation, is 69 days [tp = 69 days] when measured at the body temperature characteristic of active individuals, which is 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The attainment of puberty at just over two months of age enables first-year birds to participate in the subsequent breeding season, a life-history strategy that maximizes lifetime fecundity in a short-lived, high-mortality environment. Some variation in this timing has been noted across elevational gradients, with individuals in colder, less productive sites occasionally delaying maturation slightly, reflecting a plastic response to local resource availability and thermal conditions.
